title: EditText: Structure-Aware Generation and Selective Visual Transport for Fine-Grained Text Editing
abstract: Fine-grained text editing aims to accurately replace text in a specified region while preserving the source text's font, color, and texture, as well as visual consistency in unedited regions. We present EditText, a unified framework for fine-grained text editing that combines target character generation with visual transport from the source image. The model uses dual-condition Fill inputs: a masked image and a source text style reference, both sharing a spatial reference with the target image. The masked image hides the original text and retains unedited content as a source canvas; the style reference supplies appearance cues that guide new character generation together with the target text. We introduce an Attention Transport framework in which Source Weight describes the attention allocated to a condition and the Spatial Aggregation Kernel describes its internal spatial attention distribution. Accurate transfer of source details depends on attention strength, the retention of details in condition features, and spatially accurate aggregation. For selected non-edit queries, we therefore preserve the total attention weight assigned to the masked image while redistributing its attention toward spatially corresponding neighborhoods, enabling selective visual transport. Multi-stage training, combined with a Glyph-aware Structural Loss on local target character structure, teaches the model to generate accurate text, preserve source text appearance, and retain unedited details. We also introduce TBench, a fine-grained text editing benchmark covering Alphabetic, Logographic, and Arabic numerals, to evaluate character updates, appearance preservation, and the preservation of unedited details. On TBench, EditText achieves state-of-the-art non-edit-region SSIM (0.9769) and full-image LPIPS (0.0460).

title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models
abstract: Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss. As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.

title: Separating Environment and Sensor Shift from Acquisition Protocol in Physical Vision Benchmarks
abstract: In real-world deployments, vision systems must operate under varying environmental conditions, such as illumination changes. Recent work has explored adaptive sensing strategies that select camera parameters according to the current environment and downstream task to improve task performance. Reliable physical benchmarks are therefore essential for evaluating such strategies. We study ImageNet-ES-Diverse, a physical benchmark that evaluates the adaptive exposure control strategy Lens by recapturing printed ImageNet images under varying illumination conditions. We construct four controlled acquisition pipelines that vary printed-image scale and camera zoom, and conduct a pilot study with directly captured physical objects. We find that the acquisition choices substantially change benchmark difficulty on all downstream baselines. Moreover, the average classification-accuracy advantage of Lens over auto exposure observed on the original benchmark does not persist in either our collected pipelines or real-object pilot study. Oracle exposure selection nevertheless retains substantial gains, indicating remaining potential for sensor control. These findings highlight acquisition protocol as an important factor in physical benchmark evaluation and motivate explicit protocol reporting and evaluation across multiple acquisition setups when assessing adaptive-sensing benefits.

title: 3D Tracking Any Point with Events and Frames
abstract: Tracking a fast-moving point in 3D is prohibitive when RGB frames are blurred or too far apart to reveal its motion. Event cameras record brightness changes between frames, providing measurements inside these temporal gaps. We introduce TrackAnyMotion, which combines monocular RGB frames and events to track arbitrary points in 2D and 3D, including at times when no RGB frame is available. The motion expected for a static point, given scene geometry and camera motion, provides a reference for identifying independently moving objects. An independent-motion decoder combines geometric motion cues with event guidance and 2D tracks, feeding its predictions back into iterative 2D and 3D refinement. We also introduce HyperEvent, a synthetic RGB--Event dataset with high-frequency 3D trajectories, geometry, and independent-motion labels. At RGB frame timestamps on this benchmark, TrackAnyMotion reduces 3D and 2D endpoint errors by 70\% and 32\%, respectively.

title: ShapeQuest: Towards Granularity-Controlled Edit-Conditioned 3D Asset Retrieval
abstract: Given a reference asset and an instruction such as "remove one armrest," a retriever must find variants that make the edit and preserve the other parts. This search is well established for images but remains underexplored for individual 3D assets. To study this problem, we introduce ShapeQuest and ShapeQuester, a new benchmark and model for edit-conditioned 3D asset retrieval. ShapeQuest's open-source pipeline edits textured meshes through part additions, removals, and material and colour changes. It controls edit granularity across five levels, defined by the fraction of the object's surface area each edit affects. It constructs multiple valid targets when an instruction leaves the choice of part open. A vision-language model judges each edit from views chosen to expose the edited parts, and human raters audit its judgments. ShapeQuest has 87,824 queries in 50 categories and a 50,919-shape gallery with competing edits. To distinguish these variants, ShapeQuester learns retrieval alongside reconstruction of the edited point cloud, with part masks supervising changed and preserved regions. With a frozen pretrained point encoder, ShapeQuester reaches 50.4 operation-macro mAP@10 on the test split, against 47.2 for the fusion baseline with the same inputs and 48.6 for the strongest baseline. Reconstruction adds 6.5 points on the validation split when the point encoder is trained from scratch, including 3.3 from part masks.

title: Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
abstract: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.

title: Rethinking Reasoning Effort Training in Large Language Models: On-Policy Distillation or Reinforcement Learning?
abstract: Large language models have shown strong capabilities on complex tasks, yet how to control their reasoning effort remains a significant challenge for practical deployment. This paper provides a systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training, contrasting reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). We find that compressing reasoning and separating effort tiers are governed by different signals. Length-penalized RL reliably compresses a single policy, reducing thinking on AIME25 by 70\% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained jointly. Multi-teacher OPD separates them: across 33 benchmarks, low and medium use 58\% and 43\% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves on the reference policy by 3.1 points. We trace this difference to the training signal. A sequence-level reward cannot tell tier-specific behavior from shared behavior, whereas OPD supplies a tier-specific target at every visited state, including the decision to stop. Building on this analysis, we show that a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is sufficient to learn separated tiers within one RL stage, and that natural-language effort instructions make this separation emerge from the start of training, yielding a policy competitive with multi-teacher OPD at matched thinking length. Finally, the separation built by dense targets holds only on the states seen in training: it does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort acts mainly through the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression induced by sequence-level rewards does.

title: Your VLM Knows What to Inspect: Semantic Probe-Guided Adaptive Focusing for GUI Grounding
abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.

title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
abstract: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.

title: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies
abstract: Face Verification (FV) systems have exhibited remarkable performance in verification tasks and have consequently garnered extensive adoption across various applications, from identity duplication to authentication in mobile payments. However, the surge in popularity of face verification has raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities in the face of adversarial attacks. These concerns originate from the fact that advanced FV systems, which rely on deep neural networks, have recently demonstrated susceptibility to crafted input samples known as adversarial examples. Although imperceptible to human observers, adversarial examples can deceive deep neural networks during the testing and deployment phases. These vulnerabilities raised significant concerns about the deployment of deep neural networks in safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive investigations into adversarial attacks and corresponding defense strategies. This comprehensive survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep face verification, encompassing a broad spectrum of topics such as algorithmic designs, database utilization, protocols, and application scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of state-of-the-art algorithms to generate adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms devised to mitigate such adversarial threats.

title: Adaptive Electromagnetic Transient-level Digital Twins for Data Centers via In-Context Learning with LLMs
abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads has significantly increased data center (DC) power demand. Frequent operational and configurational changes, such as load surges caused by dynamic workload allocation, can induce electromagnetic transients (EMTs) whose accurate prediction is critical for reliable DC operation and maintenance. Although high-fidelity EMT solvers are widely adopted for transient analysis, their computational cost limits large-scale and multi-scenario studies. Digital twins address this computational bottleneck by emulating the behavior of a physical system and enabling fast prediction in place of expensive high-fidelity simulation. However,data-driven digital twins are non-adaptive and fail to generalize once the DC configuration changes. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an adaptive EMT-level digital twin for DCs based on in-context learning (ICL) with large language models (LLMs). We formulate the EMT prediction task as a system identification problem under parametric uncertainty and develop a GPT-2-based framework that adapts to unseen DC configurations at inference time from a small set of EMT trajectory samples, without model retraining. The proposed framework is validated on three representative EMT scenarios and benchmarked against three baseline non-adaptive twins. Results demonstrate superior prediction accuracy, improved adaptability to unseen operating conditions, and substantial computational speedups compared to high-fidelity EMT simulation.

title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters
abstract: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.

title: TQ-HQNet: A Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for Cross-Domain Learning on Heterogeneous Data
abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks are a promising direction for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing, but their practical effectiveness is often limited by poor trainability, rigid circuit design, and weak robustness across heterogeneous real-world tasks. This paper proposes TQ-HQNet, a Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for cross-domain learning on heterogeneous data. The proposed framework combines three mechanisms: 1) adaptive latent compression to map domain-specific features into qubit-compatible representations, 2) trainability-aware search over compact variational circuit candidates, and 3) hybrid fusion of multiple shallow quantum experts to improve robustness without increasing qubit cost excessively. TQ-HQNet is evaluated on four public datasets spanning neurological screening, phishing detection, financial direction prediction, and DNA sequence classification. Across all domains, the proposed model consistently improves over a fixed hybrid quantum baseline, with balanced-accuracy gains of +0.280, +0.170, +0.071, and +0.060, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity studies confirm that gains arise from trainability-aware compact circuit selection and expert fusion, not circuit scaling. Although classical baselines outperform on some tasks, fixed-split results show consistent improvements over the fixed hybrid reference. These analyses support the practical role of compact selection and fusion, with repeated-split and hardware-aware studies left for future work.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.

title: Simultaneously Boosting Efficiency and Capability for Linear Attention via Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification
abstract: Self-attention's quadratic complexity constitutes a core bottleneck for Vision Transformers (ViTs). Existing efficiency-oriented optimizations, including softmax-based and linear attention (LA) variants, generally compromise model representational capacity, leading to inevitable performance degradation. We propose a novel linear attention which alleviates this efficiency-capability dilemma. For the first time, we embed an Adaptive Channel Compression and Activation Purification (ACCAP) mechanism into the QKV projection of linear attention, which enables the model to retain high-dimensional feature information while performing computations with reduced channels. We further fuse a focused kernel function and a self-gating module into ACCAP to construct a lightweight linear attention module (ACCAP-LA). Our theoretical analysis shows that, compared to standard linear attention, ACCAP-LA reduces the attention module's parameter count by 79.17% and FLOPs by 77.5%. Extensive experiments demonstrate ACCAP-LA's effectiveness: when applied to ViT, it achieves 79.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with only 5.8M parameters, and more notably, it boasts strong cross-architecture compatibility, boosting EfficientViT-b1 and PVT-T by 3.3% and 3.4% respectively.

title: When "Neutral" Means Irrelevant: A Construct-Validity Audit of NormAd-ETI
abstract: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way score measures. It combines two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. Separating them shows that when only a country is shown, applicability falls to near chance while conformity stays well above it, because the prompt withholds the rule a Neutral label depends on. Because one answer carries both decisions, the score follows the steadier conformity and hides the weaker applicability, and no single prompt recovers the two separately. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate them for frontier models but not for small open models, where the applicability judgment still tracks the hidden acceptability label. Adding a written rationale reduces that conflation without removing it. We recommend reporting the two results separately and measuring the conflation gap.

title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows
abstract: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. title: EnSurv: Deep Generative Survival Modeling with Application to Kidney Graft Outcomes
abstract: Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for life-threatening end-stage renal disease, providing significant survival advantages over dialysis. Given the severe shortage of donor organs, accurately predicting the time to premature graft failure is an essential clinical task for optimizing organ allocation and tailoring individualized immunosuppressive therapies. This study is motivated by a comprehensive United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) dataset containing 243,443 kidney transplant records with complex multi-region structures and high right-censoring rates. We propose EnSurv (survival engression), a deep generative survival framework designed to capture complex, non-linear clinical covariate interactions for modeling time to graft failure. Within a pre-additive noise model (pre-ANM) family, EnSurv optimizes an energy score augmented with pooled Kaplan-Meier tail completion to handle right-censoring. We identify the pooled-completion target of the objective, establish consistency for its best approximation within the pre-ANM family, and give conditions and error bounds for its relation to true conditional graft survival. EnSurv also provides global explainability through summaries of fitted feature weights and incorporates domain constraints through established clinical directions using a soft gradient penalty. Extensive simulation experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method in comparison with existing methods. Application to the UNOS cohort demonstrates that EnSurv effectively models individual and region-level effects, consistently outperforming baselines across evaluation metrics encompassing discrimination, calibration, and accuracy.

title: OrangeTree: A Linear and Tree-based Time Series Forecasting Model Supporting Multiple Input and Output Lengths
abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) models suffer from a critical rigidity: the inability to handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) within a single architecture. Current workarounds, such as padding or autoregression, often incur computational redundancy or suffer from error accumulation. We propose OrangeTree, a linear and tree-based architecture that decouples model parameters from sequence lengths. It employs a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder to translate multi-length input history into multi-length output predictions within a unified framework. Crucially, a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser bridge these components, dynamically selecting and fusing relevant ranges into optimal contexts for forecasting. Experiments on six benchmarks confirm OrangeTree achieves the SOTA performance. In MIOL settings, it matches the accuracy of length-fixed models without substantial accuracy degradation or a substantial increase in inference latency typical of heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Tang-Yiqi/OrangeTree.

title: A 3D Simulator for Passive SPAD Imaging
abstract: Passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras provide short-exposure observations for low-light perception, but collecting task annotations for these sensors remains difficult, and annotated datasets are scarce. We present a 3D simulation pipeline that generates realistic photon detections together with camera-motion and semantic labels, enabling perception models to be trained on synthetic SPAD observations and applied directly to real-world data. The pipeline couples controllable scene geometry and motion with a sensor-informed observation model that accounts for photon shot noise, dark counts, and spatial crosstalk. We evaluate the pipeline through calibrated photon-count comparisons and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across three downstream perception tasks. We show that classifiers trained only on synthetic SPAD data achieve high accuracy on real low-light recordings at illumination levels less than 2 lux, without real-data fine-tuning. Similarly, we apply models trained entirely on simulated camera sweeps to real-world camera-rotation estimation and achieve mean absolute rotation errors of less than 1 degree on real 20-degree and 30-degree sweeps at 0.5 and 5.0 lux, when deployed zero-shot. We additionally train semantic segmentation models on synthetic data with automatically generated dense labels and perform direct inference on real-world low-light recordings; the results further demonstrate the usefulness of synthetic dense supervision for real low-light perception. Our simulator thus provides a practical source of annotated training data for real SPAD perception.

title: MemHand: Memory-Enhanced World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
abstract: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. We will release our code and models at the project page: https://irmvlab.github.io/memhand.github.io

title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
abstract: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.

title: Sub-Riemannian structure for Oriented Point Clouds
abstract: Many frameworks dealing with 3D (oriented) point clouds define locality in the ambient Euclidean space: $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs and radius balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are critical to define which points are "close to one another" and should exchange information. This can unintentionally merge sampled surfaces that are close in space but geometrically distinct such as the two faces of a thin leaf. Then, features are more prone to leak across boundaries which hinder performance. To address this, we propose to define a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$: points are lifted to $(x,n)$ with $n$ a surface normal, and "motion" is constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution in which spatial velocity must stay in the plane orthogonal to the normal which can reorient at a cost. From this, we derive an explicit score, which locally approximate the distance, to compare oriented points for downstream tasks. We report improved segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contact when using the score as a drop-in change inside PointNet++ aggregation mechanism as well as reduced leakage when using it to simulate heat diffusion on oriented points.

title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering
abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.

title: Beyond Expert Replay: Cross-Instruction Anchoring for Continual Vision-Language-Action Learning
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.

title: Loss of Approval Validity After Critical Evidence Removal in Construction QA/QC - Reproducibility Dataset
abstract: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility dataset, experimental protocols, execution scripts, policy definitions, and supplementary materials supporting the study "Loss of Approval Validity After Critical Evidence Removal in Construction QA/QC". The study evaluates Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4.1-mini using 28 synthetic construction QA/QC evidence packs, five controlled evidence states (T0, E1, E2, E6, and E7), and six requirement-level decisions per state. The frozen primary experiment comprises 280 archived API responses and 1,680 requirement-level acceptance decisions. Repository contents The deposit includes the frozen experimental dataset, author-defined policy oracle, primary estimand specifications, execution and scoring scripts, archived model responses, supplementary analyses, and integrity-verification materials. Primary evaluation outcomes The study evaluates policy-validity loss under role-critical documentary evidence removal relative to a policy-irrelevant control intervention. The study-defined Intervention-Validity Contrast (τ_IVC) was 0.0476 for Gemini 2.5 Flash and 0.1012 for GPT-4.1-mini. Across all five evaluated evidence states, unsafe automatic approvals totalled 26 for Gemini and 17 for GPT. Reproducibility and limitations The primary results are preserved in a frozen reproducibility archive with SHA-256 integrity checks. Supplementary analyses include offline rule-gating assessments, a multi-run sensitivity experiment, and an exploratory control analysis. The benchmark uses synthetic construction records and an author-defined policy oracle. The study does not establish independent engineering validation, production deployment suitability, or real-world construction safety. Exact replay of hosted LLM outputs is not guaranteed. title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

title: ST-GNN-AAAS: Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection in the Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection (AAAS) aims to make solver choices under varying time budgets. The existing AAAS approaches largely rely on static instance characteristics and make limited use of temporal information revealed during solver execution. We propose ST-GNN-AAAS, a Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network framework for AAAS in the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). The framework represents evolving incumbent tours using time-varying node features, including distances from each node to its neighbors in the current tour, and combines these features with solver performance observations over a short history window. Given this short history, ST-GNN-AAAS predicts solver selections over a longer future horizon. We evaluate the method on a subset of diverse TSP benchmarks from NATIONAL, TNM, TSPLIB, and VLSI, releasing the corresponding solver execution data to support reproducibility. Our model achieves a selection accuracy of 76.59% and closes 46.05% of the average rank gap between the single best solver (SBS) and the virtual best solver (VBS).

title: Characterizing Datasets to Anticipate Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Performance for Radiographic Pneumonia Detection
abstract: Deep learning models for pneumonia detection from chest radiographs exhibit degraded accuracy when applied across institutions, which motivates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). We observe that UDA performance depends on the properties of both the source and target datasets, and that performance gains are asymmetric with respect to dataset pairs. We investigate which structural properties of chest X-ray datasets are the most important predictors of UDA performance, and whether they can be measured before adaptation is attempted. title: Monte Carlo Tree Search for Classifier Chains
abstract: Multi-label classification continues to be relevant to a variety of modern tasks. Among other challenges, modern data sets are increasingly large with respect to the number of labels, and these labels may be noisy or missing in the training sets. Label-wise scores and ranking-based metrics have been popular, but optimising exact multi-label evaluation (where a predicted set of labels should match the true set exactly) is particularly relevant for many domains, e.g., in medicine; alongside some measure of confidence. This requires an estimation of joint probability across labels (a model of label dependence; conditioned on each input instance). A family of methods known as probabilistic classifier chains provides such inference. However, these existing varieties either do not scale to a large number of labels or do so by approximating joint via marginal distributions in a way that compromises the estimation of uncertainty for exact match accuracy. We overcome this issue by proposing TSCC; leveraging a Monte Carlo Tree Search methodology to enhance chain inference via an efficient balance between the exploration of label space and the exploration of promising label-set predictions. Results are promising both in terms of predictive and computational performance.

title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.

title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.

title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

title: RFW-W: Scaling Physical Asset Universes for Generative Embodied Simulation
abstract: Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.

title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.

title: Gated Concept Adapters: Layer-Wise Concept Bottlenecks for Auditable Text Understanding
abstract: Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.

title: Implementation of Machine Translation for the Uzbek Language Based on Transformer Models
abstract: This research focuses on building a machine translation system for the Uzbek language using transformer models such as T5 and mT5. Because of the limited data and the complexity of the Uzbek language, we collect, preprocess and augment data to create a strong Uzbek-English parallel corpus of about 3 million sentence pairs. The models are fine-tuned for optimal translation performance, and we use the BLEU score to evaluate the results. This study shows that our approach significantly improves upon older methods and helps promote the Uzbek language in the digital world.

title: The Old Scene Lives in the Cache: Diagnosing and Shedding Stale History in Streaming Video Generation
abstract: Switching scenes while preserving the original subject in streaming video generation exposes a conflict: cached history helps maintain the subject but also sustains old-scene objects that should disappear. Through controlled interventions on text conditioning, denoising steps, the local window, and the attention sink, we identify how cached visual history keeps this obsolete content. When the original frames remain in the cache, KV flush and sink recomputation still leave old-scene objects in the generated videos. Replacing this history with target-scene history largely removes those objects, but also changes the subject, reducing face similarity to the pre-switch subject. We then propose Molt Forcing, a training-free method that rebuilds scene history from a cold-start target scene while selectively retaining subject tokens from the original cache. Across 16 scene families, Molt Forcing removes old-scene objects at least as reliably as an Echo-Forcing hard cut while keeping the subject much closer to its pre-switch appearance.

title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
abstract: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $δ$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.

title: EvOrderBench: When do sampled frames establish event order?
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.

title: FERRETS: A Scalable Symbolic Transform for Time Series Classification
abstract: Dictionary methods for time series build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. Against other families of methods, their accuracy no longer pays for their cost. We present FERRETS, a label-free dictionary transform built on WEASEL~2. It keys windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a level word of each window's mean and spread, and on multivariate data adds cross-channel words. We compare it with leading classifiers, deep networks and foundation models included, on the UCR, Multiverse and MONSTER archives. FERRETS is the fastest of the eleven methods timed on UCR under a ten-thread budget. Of the ten others, only MultiRocket-Hydra is significantly more accurate, taking 24.7 times as long. title: On the Effectiveness of Resampling for Supervised Graph Anomaly Detection
abstract: Class imbalance and scarce anomaly labels motivate oversampling in supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), but its benefits across detectors and benchmarks remain unclear. In the low-label setting of GADBench, with 20 labelled anomalies and 80 labelled normal nodes, we compare class weighting and up to six oversampling strategies in ten detector configurations from three families: graph neural networks (GNNs), tree ensembles on neighbourhood-aggregated features, and tabular foundation models, on 17 datasets. On the eight datasets with organic anomalies, no strategy has a statistically resolved average gain in any configuration, and which nodes are labelled matters as much as the strategy. On the nine datasets with injected anomalies, Gaussian-noise oversampling (ROSE) gains up to 5.2 AUPRC points in four of the six tree and tabular foundation model configurations, and in all six only on attribute-swap anomalies; in four GNNs its gain is not distinguishable from zero. This gain depends on the injection recipe, which gives swapped nodes an atypical feature norm: it is no longer distinguishable from zero when the swap uses a single random donor or preserves the norm, although most detectors then also stop detecting the swaps. Over the 17 datasets, tuning the tree detectors adds about three points, as much as ROSE, and cuts ROSE's gain by about half or more. With the same source nodes and class weight, sampled graph views are not distinguishable from plain copies of those nodes. We recommend tuning baselines, repeating labelled splits, reporting organic and injected anomalies separately, and checking label-free degree and feature-norm baselines.

title: CriticJEPA: World Models Are Better Critics Than Optimizers
abstract: Visual world models enable goal-directed planning by predicting action outcomes. Gradient-based planners optimize actions to lower predicted goal cost, but continued optimization can exploit prediction errors after execution stops improving. Comparing plans requires informative relative scores; improving them also requires reliable update directions. Exact-state execution reveals that a frozen hierarchical world model ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative. Effective planning pairs goal-directed candidates with predictions that distinguish their outcomes. We introduce CriticJEPA, which learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level. Forward selection forms a complete planner; short anchored updates refine candidates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation, CriticJEPA increases success at a fraction of the planning compute, transferring shared settings across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks while keeping every world-model weight fixed.

title: An Automated Framework Integrating Deep Learning and Anatomical Reasoning for Cardiac Phenotyping From CCTA
abstract: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) depicts coronary anatomy and cardiac fat, but segmentation alone does not ensure anatomically consistent measurements. We propose an automated framework that combines deep learning with anatomical reasoning for quantitative cardiac phenotyping. Its anatomical measurement module uses graph geometry, branch identity, and surrounding structures to define vessel-specific pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) sampling and a surrogate epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) compartment. The latter also generates training targets without requiring expert pericardium contours. A companion module quantifies coronary calcium on non-contrast CT. Component-wise benchmarking was conducted on five public datasets: ImageCAS, ImageCAS-X, COCA, Visual Lab, and MultiD4CAD. On ImageCAS-X Test-160, lumen segmentation with validation-selected post-processing achieved a Dice score of 0.9133 and a clDice score of 0.940, exceeding the corresponding published CAS-Net point estimates. In the four-split ImageCAS evaluation, the four-member ensemble outperformed the single ResEnc-L model. Analysis of 800 paired scans showed that PCAT attenuation measurements differed between whole-vessel and lumen references. External EAT evaluation showed strong volume correlation and good spatial overlap. Explicit anatomical rules make the resulting measurements interpretable and inspectable. In practice, the framework provides a standardized pipeline for processing cardiac CT cohorts and quantifying coronary calcium, PCAT, and EAT for population-level analysis and comparison across studies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/HarryTRAN207/CardiacCT-Research

title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.

title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
abstract: The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain). Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined). We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal. Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.

title: GREMLIN: Generating Random Environments for Meta-Learning with Interacting Networks
abstract: Can randomly parameterized neural environments supply useful experience for learning a reinforcement learning algorithm? We investigate this question using DiscoRL's rule-discovery framework, replacing human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments. Each game combines bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward. After 224.8 million agent-environment steps, we froze the teacher and trained fresh agents. DQN outscored GREMLIN on most games, both generated and human-designed. GREMLIN nevertheless outperformed the untrained teacher on all 26 games, showing that generated experience can improve a learning rule. It remains unclear whether this approach can yield a competitive rule with longer meta-training.

title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
abstract: We prove that the following problem is NEXPTIME-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and truncated ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.

title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models
abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 < 0$). We present PhysRF-WorldJEPA, a manifold-decoupled Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates continuous electromagnetic state prediction from cross-modal language alignment. An unattenuated 1.0x clock anchor and parallel dual-scale RF encoder feed a lean ~3% LoRA LLM trained with two-step state-space EMA-JEPA (Denoise -> Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.

title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion
abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).

title: The Geometry Is the Memory: Task-Density Routing for Continual LoRA
abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. We propose CONTLORA, which replaces stored examples with compact class statistics for adapter selection and classification. Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select LoRA adapters, while accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Trained without retaining images or feature vectors, CONTLORA reaches 88.55% accuracy on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200. Across three benchmarks in the matched component study, its mean final accuracy differs from an independently trained stored-feature counterpart by at most 0.07 percentage points. Ablations show that improved task coverage need not improve classification and adapter composition also matters. On held-out classes, competitor-centered likelihood scores improve novelty AUROC over raw likelihood without altering routing ranks. These results support statistical memory as an alternative to example-retention approaches in the evaluated settings, while identifying task ambiguity as an ongoing limitation.

title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

title: Weight Scale Rebalancing: Transferable Training Recipes for Transformers
abstract: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $σ$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.
